title: King Sivi's eyes
hookLine: a king gives his eyes to a blind beggar (Jataka 499)

lines: A BLIND MAN ASKS FOR AN EYE.
cards: Some gifts cost nothing. Spare change, an old coat, a favor that fits the afternoon. King Sivi, in the Jataka, had given plenty of those: food, clothes, money, the story says, and he still wanted to give more.
One day he made a quiet wish: if anyone ever asked for a part of his own body, he would give it. Then someone asked. A blind old man came before the king and asked for an eye.

teach.h: A BEGGAR WHO WASN'T A BEGGAR.
teach.b: First, the test. The blind man wasn't what he seemed. The Jataka says he was Sakka, king of the gods, in disguise, come to see whether Sivi meant his wish.
The king's ministers pleaded: give gold, give jewels, give anything, but not your eyes. Sivi sent for his surgeon anyway. The story doesn't hurry here.
It dwells on the pain, and has the king say he gives not for gain but for the sake of awakening. Once the first eye was given, he gave the second. Third, the aftermath.
Blind now, Sivi left the palace and sat alone by a pond. Sakka came back and asked him to speak the truth about his gift. The king said, truthfully, that he had given gladly.
On those true words, the story says, his sight returned. Fourth, how to hold a story this extreme. It isn't a recipe for harming yourself.
If you're having thoughts like that, please pause and reach out: call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Tradition tells it as a picture of the perfection of giving, dana, stretched as far as it can go.
Its question for an ordinary Tuesday is smaller and sharper: is there a gift that would actually cost you something?
An hour you'd guarded. Credit you'd love to keep. An apology that bruises your pride.
Sivi's tale isn't about the size of a gift. It's about giving past the part of you that would rather hold back.

how: The Sivi story is told in Buddhist teaching as an example of the perfection of giving (dana); everyday generosity takes smaller forms, like food offered to monastics, gifts to people in need, or time given freely.

o: a sacrifice made to win favor
a payment owed to a temple

games.q: who's who in King Sivi's story: tap the pairs.
p: Sakka, king of the gods, in disguise
begged him to give gold instead

s: in the story, Sivi gives only one eye
once the first eye is given, he gives the second as well.
the blind man was a god testing the king
the Jataka says Sakka came in disguise to see whether Sivi meant his wish.
Sivi stays blind for the rest of his life
after he speaks the truth about his gift, the story says his sight returns.

games.q: you're King Sivi. your ministers beg you to give gold instead of your eye. what do you do?
o: give gold, and keep your eyes.
send for the surgeon and give the eye.
ask the blind man to come back another day.
games.why: he sends for the surgeon over every protest, and gives both eyes; the tale is told as giving stretched to its limit.

practice: Ask yourself quietly what you could give that you'd rather keep: time, attention, a word of credit, patience with someone who wears yours thin. Don't pick the biggest answer; pick the one that's real.
Then rest a while and simply notice the part of you that wants to hold on, without arguing with it.

wordCard.voice: Dana. Giving: the perfection King Sivi showed, a gift given whole, what he would most want to keep, asked for nothing back. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit dana, giving: the perfection Sivi's tale is told to show.

carryVoice: Your line: what he gave. He gave it gladly, and asked nothing back. See you tomorrow.
